clusters.parent_theme: Computational complexity of curing the sign problem
clusters.canonical_title: Complexity of curing the sign problem with constant-depth circuits allowing two-qubit rotations
clusters.canonical_statement: What is the computational complexity of deciding whether a local Hamiltonian can be cured — transformed into a stoquastic, sign-problem-free form — by a constant-depth quantum circuit that also allows two-qubit rotations, whether discrete or continuous?
clusters.scope: The curing decision problem for local Hamiltonians under the transformation class of constant-depth quantum circuits that may include two-body rotations (discrete or continuous); the complexity classification (membership, hardness, or efficient algorithm) for this richer class, which the source paper explicitly leaves open after proving NP-completeness only for single-qubit Clifford and orthogonal transformation classes.

source_support.exact_excerpt: It is important to clarify the computational complexity of finding the curing transformation in the case of constant-depth circuits that also allow two-body rotations, whether discrete or continuous.

aliases: Curing transformation complexity for constant-depth circuits with two-qubit rotations
clusters.verification_plan: A submitted answer must be a complexity classification of the stated decision problem for the stated transformation class: either a membership/hardness proof (e.g., NP-completeness or containment in a named class) via a rigorous reduction, or a polynomial-time algorithm for finding curing transformations under constant-depth circuits with two-qubit rotations together with a correctness and runtime proof, or a rigorous impossibility/conditional-hardness result. It passes if the argument is mathematically rigorous and addresses exactly the transformation class of constant-depth circuits allowing discrete or continuous two-body rotations, without silently reverting to single-qubit-only transformations.
clusters.decomposition_rationale: The source record's conclusions section explicitly lists two separable open questions; this candidate isolates the first one (the transformation-class question: constant-depth circuits with two-body rotations) from the second (reducing locality to 2-local building blocks), which is kept as its own candidate. No restriction beyond the source's stated class and decision-problem framing is added.
clusters.rationale: The authors themselves flag this as an important unresolved extension of their hardness results; the lead restates it without strengthening, and the decision-problem framing yields an unambiguous acceptance standard.

clusters.parent_theme: Computational complexity of curing the sign problem
clusters.canonical_title: Extending NP-completeness of sign-problem curing to 2-local Hamiltonians
clusters.canonical_statement: Can the NP-completeness of finding curing transformations — proven for 3-local Hamiltonians under tensor products of single-qubit Clifford gates and for 6-local Hamiltonians under general single-qubit orthogonal rotations — be extended to 2-local Hamiltonians?
clusters.scope: The locality of the hardness constructions for the curing decision problem: whether the known NP-completeness results (3-local under single-qubit Clifford transformations; 6-local under single-qubit orthogonal transformations) can be reduced to 2-local building blocks, as the source paper explicitly poses as an open question.

source_support.exact_excerpt: Also, since our NP-completeness proof involved 333 and 666-local Hamiltonians, it is interesting to try to reduce it to 222-local building blocks.

aliases: Locality reduction for computational stoquasticity hardness
clusters.verification_plan: A submitted answer must settle the complexity of the curing decision problem at locality 2 under the paper's stated single-qubit transformation classes: either an NP-hardness/NP-completeness proof for 2-local Hamiltonians via an explicit rigorous reduction, or a polynomial-time algorithm with correctness proof showing the 2-local case is tractable, or a rigorous barrier/conditional result. It passes if the argument is mathematically rigorous, uses 2-local Hamiltonians throughout (not higher-local gadgets with unproven reductions), and keeps the paper's transformation classes and decision-problem framing.
clusters.decomposition_rationale: The source record explicitly separates this locality-reduction question from the transformation-class question; each is an independent research target with its own acceptance standard, so the record is split along that source-supported boundary. The ar5iv digit renderings (333/666/222) are preserved verbatim in the excerpt; the canonical statement uses the original 3/6/2 values as documented in the record's surrounding context.
clusters.rationale: The authors' NP-completeness proofs are confined to 3- and 6-local constructions, and they name the reduction to 2-local building blocks as an explicitly interesting open direction; the candidate restates exactly that target.

clusters.parent_theme: Fundamental limits of fermionic quantum Monte Carlo
clusters.canonical_title: Fermion sign problem: existence of a polynomial-cost Monte Carlo method for quantum-degenerate fermions
clusters.canonical_statement: Can fermionic path integral Monte Carlo, or any related equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo method, compute thermal properties of quantum-degenerate fermionic systems with computing cost that does not grow exponentially with particle number N and inverse temperature beta, given that the fermion sign problem causes an exponential increase of computing time and is NP-hard in the general case?
clusters.scope: Equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo methods (PIMC and related approaches) applied to quantum-degenerate fermionic systems in full generality — no restriction to a particular model, ensemble, or temperature window; the question is whether the exponential scaling of cost with particle number and inverse temperature can be circumvented, given that a generic solution is known to be NP-hard.

authoritative_formulation.citation: M. Troyer and U.-J. Wiese, Computational Complexity and Fundamental Limitations to Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations, Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 170201 (2005), arXiv:cond-mat/0408370
authoritative_formulation.exact_excerpt: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations, while being efficient for bosons, suffer from the "negative sign problem'' when applied to fermions - causing an exponential increase of the computing time with the number of particles. A polynomial time solution to the sign problem is highly desired since it would provide an unbiased and numerically exact method to simulate correlated quantum systems. Here we show, that such a solution is almost certainly unattainable by proving that the sign problem is NP-hard, implying that a generic solution of the sign problem would also solve all problems in the complexity class NP (nondeterministic polynomial) in polynomial time.

source_support.exact_excerpt: an exponential wall in fermionic PIMC simulations with respect to N and beta, which can only be compensated by increasing the amount of compute time as ~1/sqrt(N_MC), which inevitably becomes infeasible

aliases: Negative sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo
Polynomial-time solution of the sign problem
clusters.verification_plan: A submitted answer must resolve whether sub-exponential-cost equilibrium Monte Carlo computation of thermal properties of quantum-degenerate fermions is possible: either (a) a rigorous impossibility or conditional-hardness result extending the known general-case NP-hardness to the stated setting, or (b) a constructed method with a correctness argument and a demonstrated, verified sub-exponential cost scaling in particle number N and inverse temperature beta on quantum-degenerate fermionic systems, with error bars and systematics documented. It passes if the claimed scaling or hardness holds under independent scrutiny for the general fermionic setting, not merely for a sign-problem-free special case presented as the general answer.
clusters.decomposition_rationale: The record poses a single coherent question — whether the exponential fermionic Monte Carlo cost wall can be circumvented — so no split is made. The question is kept at the source's full generality; the known NP-hardness is retained as context that bounds what a generic solution would imply, per the source's own framing, and no model subclass or temperature window is imposed.
clusters.rationale: This is the famous fermion sign problem as formulated by Troyer and Wiese; the record supplies the authoritative formulation verbatim, and the lead's restatement is equivalent in scope, preserving the source's generality while keeping the acceptance standard concrete (a scaling demonstration or a hardness proof).

clusters.parent_theme: Sign problem as a diagnostic of quantum criticality
clusters.canonical_title: Origin of the low average sign in the doped square-lattice Hubbard model
clusters.canonical_statement: What is the microscopic origin of the low average sign of the Hubbard model on the square lattice away from half-filling in determinant quantum Monte Carlo, and is its onset quantitatively linked to the onset of pseudogap behavior and exotic superconductivity?
clusters.scope: The Hubbard model on the square lattice away from half-filling as studied by determinant quantum Monte Carlo: the microscopic mechanism behind the anomalously low average sign — explicitly identified in the source as an important open problem — and the source's own proposed (unestablished) reinterpretation linking the sign onset to pseudogap and exotic-superconductivity onset.

source_support.exact_excerpt: We then propose a reinterpretation of the low average sign for the Hubbard model on the square lattice when away from half-filling, an important open problem in condensed matter physics, in terms of the onset of pseudogap behavior and exotic superconductivity.

aliases: Low average sign of the doped Hubbard model
Sign problem and pseudogap onset in the square-lattice Hubbard model
clusters.verification_plan: A submitted answer must either establish or refute the proposed reinterpretation: controlled DQMC or complementary many-body evidence demonstrating (or excluding) a quantitative correspondence between the onset of the low average sign and the onset of pseudogap behavior and exotic superconductivity in the doped square-lattice Hubbard model, with documented statistical and systematic errors; or a rigorous analysis of the model's sign structure explaining the origin of the low average sign. It passes if the claimed link (or its refutation) is supported at the level of quantitative comparison across independently computed observables, and addresses the doped square-lattice Hubbard model itself rather than a proxy model.
clusters.decomposition_rationale: The source poses one open problem (the origin of the low average sign) together with its own single proposed explanation (link to pseudogap/exotic-superconductivity onset); these form one coherent question — is the proposed reinterpretation correct — rather than an accidental conjunction, so no split is made and the model is not narrowed.
clusters.rationale: The source itself labels this an important open problem and explicitly frames its reinterpretation as a proposal, so the candidate asks for the origin and for a test of that proposal without upgrading the proposal to a conclusion.

clusters.parent_theme: Sign problem in finite-density lattice QCD
clusters.canonical_statement: Does a QCD critical point exist in the temperature–baryon-chemical-potential phase diagram, and if it does exist, what are its critical temperature and density, as established by a first-principles study based on QCD?
clusters.scope: The existence or non-existence of the QCD critical point and, if it exists, the first-principles determination of its critical temperature and density on the QCD phase diagram; the source review documents that this remains open because the sign problem at nonzero quark chemical potential defeats importance sampling and undermines current methods precisely in the relevant low-temperature, high-density region.

authoritative_formulation.citation: K. Nagata, Finite-density lattice QCD and sign problem: current status and open problems, Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. 127, 103991 (2022), arXiv:2108.12423, Sec. 1.1.1
authoritative_formulation.exact_excerpt: However, the QCD critical point has not been discovered so far. Although there are many phenomenological studies regarding the QCD critical point, the location of the critical point on the phase diagram is not known. Even the very existence is not established. The first-principle study based on QCD is needed to establish the existence or non-existence of the QCD critical point, and if it does exist, to determine the critical temperature and density.

source_support.exact_excerpt: The first-principle study based on QCD is needed to establish the existence or non-existence of the QCD critical point, and if it does exist, to determine the critical temperature and density.

aliases: Critical point of the QCD phase diagram
clusters.verification_plan: A submitted answer must be a first-principles determination: either a controlled QCD-based calculation establishing the critical point with quantified critical temperature and density and documented statistical and systematic uncertainties (including continuum and volume control appropriate to the method), or a controlled calculation excluding its existence in the relevant region of the phase diagram, or a rigorous no-go result. Phenomenological model estimates alone do not pass; the sign problem at nonzero chemical potential must be demonstrably controlled rather than assumed away, and the two components (existence, then location if existent) are reviewed as separate checkable units of the same source problem.
clusters.decomposition_rationale: The source poses existence and location as one conditional first-principles target ('establish the existence or non-existence ... and if it does exist, to determine the critical temperature and density'); splitting them would break the source's conditional structure, so they remain one candidate with separately checkable components exposed in the verification plan. The connection to the sign problem is retained as the source's documented reason the problem is open, not as an added method restriction.
clusters.rationale: This is the well-known QCD critical point problem; the review record supplies the authoritative formulation verbatim, and the lead restates it exactly, so alignment is exact with no scope modification.

clusters.parent_theme: Complexity of easing the sign problem by basis changes
clusters.canonical_title: Polynomial-time easing of the sign problem for physically motivated Hamiltonian families
clusters.canonical_statement: For which physically motivated families of quantum many-body Hamiltonians does there exist a polynomial-time classical algorithm that finds efficiently computable basis changes easing the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem, as quantified by efficiently computable measures of non-stoquasticity, given that easing in terms of those measures is NP-complete in general for nearest-neighbour Hamiltonians and simple basis choices?
clusters.scope: The complexity classification of the easing task — finding efficiently computable basis changes that reduce measurable non-stoquasticity — restricted only as the source itself frames it: the generic case is proven NP-complete ('in general ... for nearest-neighbour Hamiltonians and simple basis choices'), leaving open which structured, physically motivated Hamiltonian families admit polynomial-time easing, the regime where the paper's methodology succeeds for frustrated Heisenberg ladders.

source_support.exact_excerpt: we prove that easing the sign problem in terms of those measures is in general an NP-complete task for nearest-neighbour Hamiltonians and simple basis choices by a polynomial reduction to the MAXCUT-problem. Intriguingly, easing remains hard even in cases in which we can efficiently assert that no exact solution exists.

aliases: Tractable sign-problem easing for structured Hamiltonians
Family-specific complexity of non-stoquasticity reduction by basis changes
clusters.verification_plan: A submitted answer must classify the easing task for a specified physically motivated Hamiltonian family: either a polynomial-time algorithm that finds basis changes with a proven or quantitatively demonstrated reduction of an efficiently computable non-stoquasticity measure for that family (with runtime and improvement verified on family instances), or a family-specific hardness or impossibility proof. It passes if the claim is rigorous for the stated family, uses the paper's measure-based notion of easing, and does not rely on redefining easing or on the already-known generic NP-completeness result.
clusters.decomposition_rationale: The record poses a single classification question (which physically motivated families admit polynomial-time easing) that is left open precisely because the proven NP-completeness is explicitly qualified as generic; no split is warranted, and no particular family, geometry, or basis class is imposed beyond the source's framing.
clusters.rationale: The abstract's 'in general' qualifier and the paper's practical success on Heisenberg ladders together delimit a genuinely open boundary between tractable structured easing and generic intractability; the candidate asks exactly for that classification.
